title: What must be true about the other section's mean height?
description: Two sections of a school each have fifteen boys and fifteen girls, and the mean height of one section is given. The mean depends only on the heights in its own section, so three possible totals are tried to see what can happen to the other mean.
teaching_notes: One idea: a mean depends only on the values in its own group, so equal numbers of boys and girls do not make two means equal. Watch for children who pick the statement that the means must be the same.

video_script.why: The child can find a mean and now asks what a mean can and cannot tell.
video_script.substitution: Each section's mean depends only on that section's heights.
video_script.anchor: Two sections of the seventh grade, each with 15 boys and 15 girls; one section's mean height is 154.2 cm
video_script.payoff_line: The other section's mean cannot be determined.

final_answer.spoken: the other section's mean cannot be determined

maths_rules: the mean of one section depends only on that section's heights
each section has 15 + 15 = 30 students; first section's total 154.2 × 30 = 4626
equal numbers of boys and girls do not make heights equal
the two Grade 5 sections earlier had means 144.4 and 141.21, which differ
other totals 4500, 4626 and 4800 give means 150, 154.2 and 160: less, equal and more all fit
so nothing must be true about the other section's mean
video_script.design: Two sections drawn as equal blocks of thirty. The first block carries its total, and three different totals are tried on the second.
open_questions: The worklist writes the first Grade 5 mean as 144.5; the book says 144.4, so the script uses 144.4 with 141.21.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A school has two sections of the seventh grade.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Each section has fifteen boys and fifteen girls.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>One section's mean height is one hundred and fifty four point two centimetres.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>What must be true about the other section's mean height?

marks.m1: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Think and tell.

marks.m2: the total changes and the mean changes with it

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The mean is the total divided by the number of students.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>If the heights change, the total changes, and the mean changes with it.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>We solve it the same way as the example in your book.

beats.on_screen: Given: each section has 15 boys + 15 girls = 30 students; first section's mean = 154.2 cm
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, each section has fifteen boys and fifteen girls, thirty students in all.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The mean height of one section is one hundred and fifty four point two centimetres.

beats.on_screen: To find: what must be true about the other section's mean height

marks.m1: the question is written under the givens

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find what must be true about the mean height of the other section.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The four statements say it is equal, less, more, or cannot be determined.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, find the total height of the first section. The total is the mean times thirty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One hundred and fifty four point two times thirty is four thousand six hundred and twenty six.

beats.on_screen: other mean = other total ÷ 30; the other total depends on the other section's heights

marks.m1: other mean = other total ÷ 30 is written
marks.m2: the heights of the other section are shown as unknown

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, see what the other mean depends on. It depends only on the heights of the other section.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Fifteen boys and fifteen girls do not fix those heights.

beats.on_screen: book: two Grade 5 sections had means 144.4 and 141.21, which differ

marks.m1: the two Grade 5 means appear side by side
marks.m3: a not equal sign appears between them

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, look at your book. Two sections of the fifth grade had different means.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One was one hundred and forty four point four. The other was one hundred and forty one point two one.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Two sections of one school can have different means.

marks.m1: three totals are tried for the other section

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, try three totals for the other section.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Four thousand five hundred divided by thirty gives one hundred and fifty. Four thousand six hundred and twenty six gives one hundred and fifty four point two.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Four thousand eight hundred gives one hundred and sixty.

beats.on_screen: check: 150 × 30 = 4500; 154.2 × 30 = 4626; 160 × 30 = 4800; each section still has 30 students

marks.m1: each mean is multiplied back by 30
marks.m2: each total matches and the section still has 30 students

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step five, check the three cases. Multiply each mean back by thirty to get its total.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Each case still has fifteen boys and fifteen girls. The mean can be less, equal or more.

beats.on_screen: Answer: (d) It cannot be determined; the other mean can be less, equal or more than 154.2 cm

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The other section's mean cannot be determined.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It can be less than, equal to or more than one hundred and fifty four point two. The fourth statement is the right one.
